articles.title: Após chuva, imóvel desaba e destroços atingem terreno de casa em Minas | G1
articles.standfirst: Ocorrência foi registrada na manhã deste domingo (11). Nas últimas 24 horas, o volume de chuva acumulado chegou a 49,3 mm em parte da cidade.
articles.summary: Ocorrência foi registrada na manhã deste domingo (11). Nas últimas 24 horas, o volume de chuva acumulado chegou a 49,3 mm em parte da cidade.
articles.body:
Imóvel abandonado desaba no Bairro Centenário, em Juiz de Fora — Foto: Contribuição do leitor

Um imóvel abandonado desabou na manhã deste domingo (11) , na Rua Vitório Saggioro, no bairro Centenário, em Juiz de Fora . Os destroços atingiram o terreno de uma casa e provocaram a queda parcial do muro de divisa da propriedade , localizada na Rua João Cardoso. A Defesa Civil esteve no local e orientou que a área próxima ao muro não seja ocupada. Ninguém se feriu.

O desabamento aconteceu após as chuvas que atingiram Juiz de Fora na noite de sábado (10). Nas últimas 24 horas, o volume acumulado chegou a 49,3 milímetros em áreas da cidade , de acordo com o balanço divulgado pela Prefeitura. O registro foi feito pela estação da Embrapa.

Ainda de acordo com a Prefeitura, as equipes da Defesa Civil atenderam cinco ocorrências na manhã deste domingo . Além do desabamento no bairro Centenário, foram registrados alagamento e infiltração em muro de contenção em outras áreas da cidade. Também foi realizada orientação técnica preventiva no Bairro Industrial.

articles.title: PMs que mataram jovem com 27 tiros após confundirem celular com arma em Moema são afastados das ruas | G1
articles.standfirst: Quatro policiais fizeram 45 disparos durante a abordagem neste sábado (10). Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, agentes confundiram o celular de Gustavo Munis de Santana com uma arma.
articles.summary: Quatro policiais fizeram 45 disparos durante a abordagem neste sábado (10). Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, agentes confundiram o celular de Gustavo Munis de Santana com uma arma.
articles.body:
Os policiais militares envolvidos na morte de Gustavo Munis de Santana , de 20 anos, foram afastados das atividades operacionais , informou neste domingo (11) a Secretaria da Segurança Pública (SSP). O jovem foi atingido por 27 tiros durante uma abordagem policial na madrugada de sábado (10), em Moema, na Zona Sul de São Paulo .

Quatro policiais fizeram 45 disparos contra o jovem. Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, os agentes confundiram o celular que Gustavo segurava com uma arma de fogo .

A SSP informou ainda que foi aberto um Inquérito Policial Militar (IPM) para apurar a conduta dos policiais e que as circunstâncias da morte também são investigadas pelas polícias Civil e Militar. O caso foi registrado no Departamento de Homicídios e de Proteção à Pessoa (DHPP).

Segundo a secretaria, as armas dos policiais e o celular de Gustavo foram apreendidos para perícia. As imagens das câmeras corporais que registraram a ação também foram solicitadas para análise.

Em nota, a SSP afirmou que “não tolera desvios de conduta dos seus agentes” e que, caso sejam constatadas irregularidades, os policiais serão punidos.

Gustavo Munis de Santana tinha 20 anos, morava com a mãe e as irmãs, trabalhava em um hospital, cuidava de cachorros e era conhecido por ajudar pessoas próximas, segundo relatos de um vizinho que o conhecia desde criança.

Gustavo Munis de Santana foi morto com 27 tiros disparado por policiais militares em SP. — Foto: Reprodução

O jovem foi morto por policiais militares com 27 tiros na madrugada de sábado (10), em Moema, Zona Sul de São Paulo. Segundo os PMs, o celular da vítima foi confundido com uma arma . Ele não tinha antecedentes criminais.

Familiares contaram aos investigadores que Gustavo lutava contra a dependência química e tomava antidepressivos desde o ano passado. No dia da ocorrência, os policiais foram acionados para atender um chamado envolvendo um "homem que estaria transtornado e ameaçava tirar a própria vida", segundo o B.O.

“É um moleque bom, gente boa, sempre que precisava ele arrumava bicicleta da minha filha”, disse o técnico de refrigeração Eguinaldo Ferreira à TV Globo.

Durante a aborgadem, quatro policiais dispararam 45 vezes contra o jovem . A perícia identificou pelo menos 27 ferimentos provocados por tiros no corpo dele.

A mãe de Gustavo esteve no local da morte durante a manhã deste sábado. Em um áudio enviado a um vizinho da família, ela relatou que estava ao lado do filho, já morto.

“Meu filho tá morto aqui na rua. Eu tô aqui sentada no meio da rua do lado dele, conversando com ele. Mas ele tá morto, ele não me responde mais. Ele não me responde”, disse.

Segundo reportagem da TV Globo, a família permaneceu no local durante a manhã e estava muito abalada. Os parentes não quiseram conceder entrevista.

O corpo de Gustavo foi liberado para o Instituto Médico Legal (IML) às 11h04, de acordo com o boletim de ocorrência. O corpo permaneceu na rua por mais de 10 horas.

Eguinaldo Ferreira afirmou à TV Globo que conhecia Gustavo desde a infância. Ele também contou que o jovem costumava ajudá-lo com pequenos consertos. Segundo ele, Gustavo também cuidava de cachorros e trabalhava em um hospital.

A Polícia Militar foi acionada pelo Centro de Operações da Polícia Militar (Copom) por volta das 2h35 para atender a uma ocorrência envolvendo um homem que estaria transtornado e ameaçava tirar a própria vida.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, quando os policiais chegaram à região da Avenida Moreira Guimarães, Gustavo correu por uma passarela em direção à Alameda dos Guaramomis e tentou se esconder no recuo de um imóvel comercial.

Os policiais relataram que o jovem saiu de uma área escura e estendeu os braços na direção deles enquanto segurava um objeto escuro. Os agentes disseram ter interpretado o movimento como uma ameaça com arma de fogo e atiraram.

A perícia encontrou ao lado do corpo um celular Samsung. O aparelho foi apreendido e será periciado.

Quatro policiais militares fizeram, juntos, 45 disparos com pistolas calibre .40 durante a ocorrência. Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, um deles informou ter disparado 14 vezes; outro, 13; um terceiro, 12; e o quarto, seis. Outros quatro policiais que estavam em viaturas de apoio não atiraram.

A perícia constatou pelo menos 27 ferimentos provocados por tiros no corpo de Gustavo. As lesões atingiram diversas regiões, incluindo cabeça, pescoço, tórax, braços, mãos, pelve e pernas.

O laudo definitivo das lesões ainda será elaborado pelo IML.

As polícias Civil e Militar investigam as circunstâncias da morte de um homem de 20 anos, ocorrida na madrugada deste sábado (10), em Moema, zona sul da capital. O caso foi registrado no Departamento de Homicídios e de Proteção à Pessoa (DHPP).

Os agentes que participaram da ocorrência foram afastados das atividades operacionais e foi aberto Inquérito Policial Militar (IPM) para apurar a conduta dos policiais. Todas os procedimentos durante e após a ocorrência serão apurados pela Secretaria de Segurança Pública.

A SSP não tolera desvios de conduta dos seus agentes e constatadas irregularidades, os profissionais serão punidos com rigor. As armas dos policiais e o celular da vítima foram apreendidos para perícia. As imagens registradas pelas câmeras corporais durante a ação também foram solicitadas para análise.

articles.title: Queimadas no Amazonas: Ministro vê cenário grave após sobrevoo | G1
articles.standfirst: Comitiva federal constatou centenas de focos criminosos no meio da floresta preservada. Em coletiva, governo anunciou reforço de 11 aeronaves e cobrou punição a incendiários.
articles.summary: Comitiva federal reforça combate às queimadas no Amazonas com 11 aeronaves após constatar focos de incêndio criminosos em áreas de floresta preservada.
articles.body:
Comitiva sobrevoa áreas afetadas por incêndios em Manaus — Foto: Paulo Roberto/Rede Amazônica

Após sobrevoar áreas atingidas por incêndios florestais no Amazonas, o ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima do Brasil João Paulo Capobianco, classificou o cenário observado na região como mais grave do que o previsto. A declaração foi feita durante entrevista coletiva na Base Aérea de Manaus (BAMN), neste domingo (11).

➡️A decolagem da aeronave da comitiva do governo federal, que estava prevista para ocorrer no início da manhã, sofreu um atraso temporário devido à densa camada de fumaça sobre Manaus, que comprometeu a visibilidade e o teto operacional na capital.

"Eu diria, mais grave do que eu imaginava depois de fazer o sobrevoo, porque nós identificamos muitos focos de incêndio no meio da floresta preservada. Não se trata apenas daquele fogo que foi colocado na pastagem e adentrou a floresta. Nesse caso, além do fogo que vem da pastagem, nós vimos focos no meio da floresta preservada. Inúmeros focos", afirmou Capobianco.

Após a melhoria das condições aeroviárias, a equipe cumpre agenda com um sobrevoo de monitoramento na região de Autazes e, na sequência, concede entrevista coletiva na Base Aérea de Manaus (BAMN) para apresentar um balanço atualizado do combate às queimadas e detalhar o envio de novos recursos ao estado.

O ministro destacou ainda que a presença de pontos de fogo isolados em áreas preservadas e de difícil acesso indica ação humana intencional para degradar o bioma e preparar o terreno para futuro desmatamento.

Diante disso, o representante da pasta fez um apelo para que o Governo do Estado empenhe a Polícia Militar ao lado do Corpo de Bombeiros no combate e na identificação dos infratores.

"É fundamental que esses indivíduos que estão agindo criminosamente vejam que serão punidos. Ou seja, é necessário combater a impunidade que está reinando aqui na região", alertou.

'Mais grave do que eu imaginava', diz ministro sobre queimadas no AM após sobrevoo em áreas afetadas — Foto: Foto: Ibama

A comitiva conta com a participação do ministro da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional, Waldez Góes; do secretário executivo do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco; do governador do Amazonas, Roberto Cidade; do presidente do Ibama, Jair Schmitt; e do secretário Nacional de Defesa Civil, Wolnei Wolff.

Antes de irem a campo, os representantes do governo visitaram o Centro Integrado de Comando e Controle (CICC) e participaram de uma reunião na sede da Superintendência da Zona Franca de Manaus (Suframa) para alinhar as ações emergenciais de resposta à crise ambiental.

Apoio aéreo, brigadas e ajuda humanitária

Para contornar o avanço das chamas, o Governo Federal confirmou a mobilização de uma frota de 11 aeronaves, incluindo aviões Air Tractor — que já realizam lançamentos de água nas áreas afetadas — e duas aeronaves C-390, que passam a operar na segunda-feira (12). Questionado sobre a permanência das equipes e equipamentos, Capobianco garantiu que o efetivo continuará no estado "até apagar os focos de incêndio que estão causando dano à população de Manaus".

Fumaça deixa qualidade do ar 'péssima' e afeta a saúde

Fumaça cobre o céu do bairro Ponta Negra, em Manaus. — Foto: Luciane Marques/Rede Amazônica

O atraso na decolagem da comitiva é reflexo da forte poluição provocada pelos incêndios na região. Pelo quarto dia consecutivo, Manaus amanheceu encoberta por uma densa fumaça.

Sensores do Sistema Eletrônico de Vigilância Ambiental (Selva), da Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA), registraram qualidade do ar “péssima” na capital e em outros cinco municípios da Região Metropolitana . No município de Careiro , os índices de concentração de partículas chegaram a 301,2 µg/m³.

Diante dos riscos à saúde humana, a Defesa Civil emitiu alerta severo orientando o uso de máscaras e a restrição de exposição ao ar livre. A Prefeitura de Manaus suspendeu todas as atividades e eventos públicos ao ar livre agendados para este domingo e para a segunda-feira (12).

Nos hospitais, a Secretaria de Estado de Saúde (SES-AM) registrou 82 atendimentos de urgência motivados por problemas respiratórios decorrentes da fumaça apenas entre os dias 1º e 8 de outubro.

Prefeitura, Estado e Governo Federal reconhecem crise

A Prefeitura de Manaus decretou estado de atenção em 24 de setembro, e a classificação segue neste domingo. Segundo o executivo municipal, o estado de atenção é adotado quando uma ou mais ocorrências afetam a cidade e há previsão de um evento de alto impacto no curto prazo.

Além da classificação da Prefeitura, Manaus foi um dos 36 municípios do Amazonas que tiveram a situação de emergência por conta dos incêndios florestais reconhecida pelo Governo Federal. O reconhecimento foi feito pelo Ministério da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional (MIDR) no sábado (10), mesmo dia em que o estado de emergência foi decretado pelo estado.

O ministro da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional, Waldez Góes, reforçou que o reconhecimento da situação de emergência nos municípios amazonenses, oficializado no sábado (10), permite a atuação integrada das forças de resposta e o repasse de recursos.

"Uma coisa é enfrentar em todas as frentes e empregar toda a força que puder, Governo Federal junto com o Estado e municípios, para apagar o fogo. A outra é assistir pessoas que já estão, de alguma forma, precisando de ajuda humanitária, de assistência médica como resultado do incêndio", pontuou Waldez Góes, destacando que equipes da Força Nacional do SUS já atuam no estado.

O decreto estadual abrange municípios da Região Metropolitana de Manaus, do sul do Amazonas e de outras regiões do estado. São eles:

articles.title: Motociclista morre em acidente em rodovia  | G1
articles.standfirst: Colisão ocorreu na noite de sábado (10). Veículo saiu de um canavial e atingiu a lateral da moto ao cruzar a pista.
articles.summary: Um acidente na SP-340 em Jaú causou a morte de um motociclista após um veículo cruzar a pista ao sair de um canavial na noite de sábado.
articles.body:
Motociclista morre em acidente na SP-340 em Jaú — Foto: CCO da Concessionária EIXO SP/Divulgação

Um motociclista morreu em um acidente na noite deste sábado (10) na Rodovia Deputado Amauri Barroso de Souza (SP-340) em Jaú (SP).

Segundo a Agência Reguladora de Serviços Públicos Delegados de Transporte do Estado de São Paulo (Artesp), a vítima trafegava pela pista quando um veículo saiu de um canavial, cruzou a faixa de rolamento e atingiu a lateral da motocicleta.

O condutor da moto não resistiu aos ferimentos e morreu no local. O motorista do outro veículo não se feriu.

Por conta do acidente e do trabalho de perícia, o acostamento da rodovia ficou interditado por cerca de três horas, mas o trecho já foi liberado.

articles.title: Damilola Taylor: Knife crime prevention needed 'now more than ever'
articles.summary: A new BBC documentary retells the story of Damilola Taylor's killing in Peckham, 26 years on.
articles.body:
The brother of schoolboy Damilola Taylor, killed in an attack in Peckham 26 years ago, has said work to tackle knife crime is "needed now more than ever".

The 10-year-old was fatally stabbed while on his way home from Peckham Library in south London on 27 November 2000.

Babatunde (Tunde) Taylor now chairs the Damilola Taylor Trust, set up by their parents in his brother's memory. It works to provide support for disadvantaged children vulnerable to falling into crime.

He said issues they were currently facing were "more diverse" than they were when his brother died.

Damilola's killing is now the subject of a BBC documentary called Damilola: The Untold Story .

Tunde said the problems faced today by young people were different to his experience growing up.

"We've got the emergence of social media... we have to find a way to keep evolving and adapting," he said.

Tunde said the charity trust was facing an uncertain future, despite its many successful programmes.

"One of the challenges we're facing is sustainability, just like every small charity there are issues regarding funding," he said.

"We're trying to keep the trust sustainable for the next generation. We're open to partnerships with people who share what we are looking to achieve.

"We need all hands on deck and we need that support to help us to continue to provide."

Damilola was born in Nigeria and moved to the North Peckham Estate with his mother and siblings in August 2000.

On 27 November, he was at Peckham Library with friends, including future actor John Boyega and Boyega's sister Grace.

While walking home, Damilola was attacked and stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle. It severed an artery.

Damilola was found in a stairwell on the estate by a caretaker and later died.

His death sent shockwaves around the country.

But convictions for his death were not secured until 2006 when two teenagers, who lived on the estate and were believed to be part of a local gang, were found guilty of manslaughter. Two previous trials had failed.

Speaking in the documentary, Boyega said the killing of his friend had a profound effect on him.

He said it had spurred him on to pursue the opportunities that were available to him, which ultimately led to him achieving his dream of becoming an actor.

"Damilola's legacy to me means being able to be unrealistic with your dreams," he said.

"He wrote a poem and he used to recite it all the time: I will travel far and wide to choose my destiny and remould the world, I know it is my destiny to defend the world, which I hope to achieve in my lifetime.

"From that poem [you can tell] he had plans and he didn't care about the environment he was in, he was more fixated on where he was going. So what's my excuse?"

Tunde said it was "very important" his brother's story was told again, more than a quarter of a century on.

"There's a whole generation of young people who were not around at the time and they get the chance to see him as a person, a young boy, his ambitions and how the tragedy cut that," he said.

"If they can think of that and think about the choices they're making then we will have actually achieved something positive."

articles.title: Firefighters spend second night at scene of Glasgow scrapyard blaze
articles.summary: The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said the alarm was raised at the business in the Scotstoun area of the city on Friday night.
articles.body:
Firefighters have spent a second night at the scene of a major blaze at a scrapyard in Glasgow.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said the alarm was raised at the business on South Street, in the Scotstoun area of the city, at about 23:23 on Friday.

One local resident captured dramatic footage of the fire at its peak, with explosive bangs emitting from an area engulfed in flames.

Nine fire engines, two high-reach vehicles and specialist resources responded to the incident. No casualties were reported.

The SFRS said crews were in attendance overnight and three appliances were still at the scene on Sunday afternoon.

During the response a high volume water pump was used to draw water from the nearby River Clyde.

The public were advised to keep windows and door closed if they could see smoke.

articles.title: Woman who clung to Spitfire during Second World War remembered
articles.summary: Margaret Horton's story is being kept alive by North Lincolnshire Heritage Centre.
articles.body:
The incredible story of a woman who hung to the tail of a Spitfire in flight is being told by volunteers at an aviation centre.

Margaret Horton was a member of the ground crew working on a Spitfire at RAF Hibaldstow, in Lincolnshire, during the Second World War when the pilot took off without realising she was on the tail. The pilot landed, Horton hopped off and went about her day.

Her story is being kept alive by North Lincolnshire Aviation Heritage Centre, which is marking seven years since work began on a visitor attraction at the former RAF site.

Phil Jones, one of the centre's directors, said visitors enjoyed discovering such tales because "it's part of who we are as human beings".

In 1945, Horton was tasked with sitting on the tail of a Spitfire while it was being taxied - a routine job used to prevent the aircraft from bouncing and the propeller striking the ground.

But when Horton was doing this, the pilot taxied out onto the runway and took off, forgetting she was still on the tail.

Speaking to the BBC in the 1970s, Horton said: "When I saw things going too fast, I flung myself across the tail plane and caught hold of the accelerator. I tried to move it so he would know I was there."

Despite clinging on to the plane for a circuit of the airfield, she survived the journey.

"He made a beautiful landing," Horton said. "It was a day to remember."

According to Jones, Horton was also told off for not getting off the tail plan and for dropping her gloves. She was made to buy some replacements.

"You would joke about it, but it must have been terrifying at the time for her," Jones said.

Horton came back decades later and recreated the famous event for the camera. A magazine clipping can be found at the heritage centre.

"It was a claim to fame, wasn't it?", Jones said.

The former RAF site was discovered completely overgrown and renovations began in 2019, but were delayed due to the Covid pandemic.

A formal opening ceremony took place in June 2024.

The site features other parts of aviation heritage throughout North Lincolnshire from World War One until the present day.

Other attractions include a replica of the famous bouncing bomb used in the Dambusters raids and the former Battle Headquarters.

The headquarters were built as an underground bunker amid fears of a German invasion following the Dunkirk evacuation.

Also on display is a Turbinlite aircraft, which used a powerful searchlight to locate and light up enemy aircraft at night so an accompanying Spitfire could shoot it down before radar became widely used.

When asked why it is important to keep these stories alive, Jones said: "Why do we do anything looking back in history? I think it's part of who we are as human beings.

"We like to know where we've come from and where we're going even though we're just passing through the middle of it.

"It's just all part of the pattern of life, isn't it?"

Volunteers look after the memorabilia and people who visit the site.

"It's a hard graft, but actually being here is an enjoyable experience," Jones said.

"We're not being paid. But it's just, it's a camaraderie.

"Doing this keeps us going. It keeps you active, keeps you fit and it keeps your brain going as well."

Speaking about his fellow volunteers, Jones said: "We've all got sort of a common interest... it just seems to click and that's part of the beauty of it."

articles.title: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
articles.summary: It is the third time this week that Ukraine has targeted Russian tech giant Yandex, forcing the company to suspend its operations.
articles.body:
Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.

The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.

Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.

Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.

Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.

The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.

The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.

Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.

On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.

Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

articles.title: A child's question at a funeral reminded us death does not get the last word
articles.summary: A five-year-old's question at his great-grandmother's funeral sparked reflections on C. S. Lewis, hospice hymns, and the hope of eternity.
articles.body: The question came unexpectedly from my five-year-old grandson. My late mom’s pastor had gathered our family to explain how her funeral service would go and asked if we had any final questions before we processed into the church. Raising his hand, my grandson inquired, "Will we see Momma Bettie again?" DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME The poignancy of his request brought tears to the eyes of almost everyone in the room. As I pondered seeing my mom again in heaven, my grandson’s query brought to mind C. S. Lewis’s famous sermon, "The Weight of Glory." Given at Oxford in 1941, Lewis posed the thought-provoking statement, "There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal." This Christian belief — that we are both image-bearers of God and have eternal existence — was the basis from which Lewis preached. And for followers of Jesus — he provided an eternal perspective — not only that our life has purpose and a higher calling, but how we should truly love those around us. As Lewis concluded his sermon, "Next to the Blessed Sacrament itself, your neighbour is the holiest object presented to your senses. If he is your Christian neighbour he is holy in almost the same way, for in him also Christ vere latitat — the glorifier and the glorified, Glory Himself, is truly hidden." This conviction informed my mom as well. For she believed the Gospel changed everything. Spending time with her during the last week of her life in hospice was both deeply sad and amazingly redemptive and beautiful. It was such a blessing to witness her saying goodbye to family and friends — as she reflected on her life, gave advice, and let the light of Christ shine forth from her as she faced death with no fear. When I asked my children to reflect on a favorite memory of my mom, they reminisced about spending time in her home — including watching movies she selected for our evening entertainment. From To Kill a Mockingbird to Anne of Green Gables to an obscure black-and-white classic, we never knew what she'd planned for us to view together. One of the most memorable films we enjoyed was Coat of Many Colors — the story of a young Dolly Parton and her family growing up in poverty in the Great Smoky Mountains of Tennessee. In fact, 13 million viewers watched the premiere on December 10, 2015 —prompting NBC to re-air the film on Christmas night that year we visited. The film was powerful not only because it showed the real pain and trials of Dolly and her family, but also because it showed redemption and reconciliation. Reflecting on Dolly's recent passing, I thought these themes, in many ways, captured my mom's heart and approach to life as a wife, mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and friend. Growing up in humble surroundings, she too looked for redemptive elements in life — whether it was family, church, community, literature, art, film, or music Along these lines, she kept an old Baptist Hymnal that she found at a garage sale with her Bible. As I was preparing for her eulogy, I found an inscription she wrote at the front: "There is great strength in these hymns. The words come to me even in my sleep. I love to wake up with a song already playing in my soul. The songs are planted in my heart through years of singing them." Flipping through the hymnal, I discovered that she had hearted the song "I Need Thee Every Hour." I now understood why, in her final days in hospice, when she barely opened her eyes, she started singing with me when I read the song "Lord I Need You, Oh I need you, Every hour I need you" from the timely Worship Initiative devotional that aired that week. It was a beautiful, powerful moment that demonstrated these songs sown in her spirit—and the hope and comfort they brought to her as she faced death. As a matter of fact, the last week in hospice showed me not only her deep love of the Lord, her family and friends, but also a heart for reconciliation. As I read through Gone From My Sight: The Dying Experience that week — provided by many hospice facilities around the country to walk through this process — I learned how "unfinished business" can be a big factor "in determining how much resistance we put into meeting death." Due to a challenging family situation, she had not seen two of her grandchildren since my father’s funeral eight years earlier. Nevertheless, when they heard about my mom’s condition, they arrived just in time to say their goodbyes. Knowing she had prayed to see them again and be reconciled, I was so thankful for the sweet time she had with both, leading her to tell my nephew that she could now die. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It would be the last conversation she had before passing two days later. In regard to my grandson’s question the afternoon of my mom’s funeral, the pastor responded beautifully, explaining that we would one day see her again — not in the feeble, frail state she had left the world — but as St. Paul described to the Church of Corinth, in her heavenly body. For "in Christ all shall be made alive…[and] raised in glory," (I Corinthians 15). CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A great comfort as we ponder the weight of eternity.

articles.title: India’s crackdown on youth protesters: What next?
articles.summary: India’s ‘cockroach’ movement and student groups have said protests will continue despite detentions.
articles.body:
India’s capital is bracing for a second day of protests after thousands of people, including the leaders of the “cockroach” youth movement and opposition politicians, were detained amid a major crackdown on demonstrators.

Abhijeet Dipke, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader, called Prime Minister Narendra Modi a “bully” shortly after he was released on Sunday. Thousands of other protesters, some of whom are members of left-wing student groups, were released on Sunday after the Supreme Court called their detention “illegal”.

“Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” Dipke said in a post on X.

The protesters are demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a revision of voter lists that they say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Modi’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Millions of voters, including Muslims, have been deleted from the rolls in a process marred by technical errors and a perceived lack of transparency.

The protests erupted across several Indian cities after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper found that two election commissioners objected to many of Kumar’s decisions. India’s Election Commission is a constitutional body with three members, and decisions are taken by majority.

What was the scale of the government crackdown?

Ahead of Saturday’s protests, the capital, New Delhi, was turned into a fortress with tens of thousands of police and paramilitary forces deployed, trains and metros suspended, and markets and major roads blocked, to prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar – a designated protest site close to India’s parliament. Jantar Mantar was sealed off.

Jantar Mantar was the site of the July protest that led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmesh Pradhan. That protest, also led by the CJP, was triggered by a string of exam paper leaks.

Security forces also set ⁠up checkpoints on major roads and entry points across the city of 20 million people, checked buses and inspected vehicles searching for protesters.

Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes.

More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the ⁠city, according to local media, and mobile internet services were suspended across several areas of the capital to stop people from online mobilisation efforts by the CJP and other youth groups.

Police detained CJP founder Dipke, as well as his associates, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, from an airplane upon arrival in New Delhi from Mumbai.

Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.”

In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke said: “This is dictatorship”.

Delhi police also detained YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist).

Some opposition politicians, as well as former chief ministers – Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala – were also detained, television channels showed.

Despite the unprecedented crackdown, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”. But police also ended up quashing these protests and detaining journalists trying to cover the demonstrations.

Besides New Delhi, some 600 people were also arrested in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, over the protests, according to the ANI news agency.

On Sunday, police officials said all detainees had been released.

The CJP leaders were released on the condition that there would be ‘no breach of peace’ for a year.

Speaking to reporters at a press conference in New Delhi on Sunday afternoon after their release, Saurav Das, the group’s co-convenor, slammed the police for “arriving like mafia dons” and “abducting” them on their plane.

After his release, Rathee said he was “KIDNAPPED.”

Several journalists from news outlets, including Scroll.in, Newslaundry and others were detained. They have all since been released, but Newslaundry said some of their reporters’ media equipment was seized during the detention.

The Committee to Protect Journalists told Al Jazeera on Saturday that it was deeply concerned by reports of journalists being temporarily detained.

“Just as police personnel are doing their jobs, journalists are also doing theirs. A free and independent press is essential to democracy,” Kunal Majumder, the CPJ’s Asia Pacific programme coordinator, said.

Aban Raza, a 37-year old visual artist based in New Delhi who was detained on Saturday, said the “entire experience has left her shocked and angry”.

“We are protesting for the right to vote. It affects all of us. So why is the police suspicious of us and treating us with so much aggression? This makes me angry,” she told Al Jazeera.

Together with three other protesters, including economist Jean Dreze, Raza managed to get close to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning.

“As soon as we reached close enough to the protest site, we started unfurling our banners which called for the resignation of Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar and for free and fair elections. But within minutes, police officials approached us, began tearing our banners and dragging us towards a bus to detain us,” she told Al Jazeera.

“We tried to resist as the police dragged us inside the bus. Both my arms feel very sore today,” she said.

Raza says that some of those detained were not even protesters.

“They were people who had just been picked up whilst they were going about their day. One person was going to the Gurudwara, another was going to meet his wife and they got detained. Most of these people were working class people,” she said.

Raza, who was released on Saturday night, said she is going back to protest on Sunday.

Youth leaders have struck a defiant note, pledging to keep up protests in New Delhi. Some members were detained on Sunday.

The group’s co-convenor Saurav Das, who was released from detention on Sunday, said in a post on X: “After Modi-Shah [Amit Shah, India’s home minister] turned Delhi into a fortress and unleashed what can only be described as a war against their own citizens, one thing has become abundantly clear: Gyanesh Kumar is at the very heart of this government’s survival.”

“But we the young generation will continue to demand accountability. We shall neither be intimidated nor silenced. We are not backing down. We are returning with full strength!” he added.

The CJP has also announced protests in other Indian cities including Mumbai for Sunday evening.

Meanwhile, Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association, began a protest on Sunday afternoon in central Delhi.

“Our peaceful protest has started at RK Ashram. Join us here and stand with us!” she said on X.

But shortly afterwards, Bora and several others were detained.

Are India’s opposition parties backing the protests?

The INDIA Bloc – India’s opposition alliance led by the Indian National Congress – has participated in protests alongside the youth-led groups, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Kumar.

The Bloc is expected to hold a protest on Monday in the capital.

“Yesterday, we held a comprehensive meeting with various leaders to prepare for this march,” Congress general secretary K C Venugopal told reporters on Saturday.

“Gyanesh must go. There will be no backing down,” he added.

Congress party leader and the leader of the opposition in parliament, Rahul Gandhi, has been spearheading a campaign against the election commissioner for months. He was briefly arrested last week over the election protest in New Delhi.

“Modi government has turned the ‘Mother of Democracy’ into a ‘Muzzled Democracy’!” Congress party president Mallikarjun Kharge posted on X.

“Detentions, arrests, jails, lathis [batons] and pellets cannot deter the people of India. Since the days of our freedom struggle, the youth have been at the forefront of shaping the nation’s destiny.”

Why is India’s government refusing to talk to the protesters?

The protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last month that two election commissioners had ⁠questioned Kumar’s revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.

The BJP says that of the 130 million names deleted from voter lists, 28 million are dead, 63 million have relocated, 10 million are duplicates and 30 million could not be traced by officials.

The ruling party has also said its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation.

But these protests have become a larger question of democracy and the right to dissent under the Modi government.

While the government had briefly engaged in talks with the youth groups during the July 2026 protests, it has taken a much more hardline stance against demands targeting constitutional and electoral authorities.

The BJP’s officials have also characterised the protests and online opposition as a concerted political effort to destabilise the government rather than highlight legitimate public grievances.

On Saturday, BJP spokesman Sambit Patra dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements” and said that “their flop show has been completely demolished”.

“What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance,” he told reporters.

Critics and analysts interviewed by Al Jazeera argue that conceding to demands for the election chief’s resignation would validate opposition accusations of vote theft and project weakness for a prime minister sensitive to his political aura.

But Sanjay Kapoor, editor of Hard News Magazine and a political analyst, told Al Jazeera on Saturday that most people coming to the protests do not want Modi’s BJP to continue to govern.

“Modi’s government has begun to lose a lot of credibility at the moment,” he said.

“BJP is afraid that the ground has shifted dramatically against them and they would find it very difficult to come back to power.”

What has been the global reactions to the protests?

On Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.

“We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” UN Human Rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement.

He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly ‌held” concerns expressed.

Amnesty International told Al Jazeera that the detentions signal the Indian government’s desperate attempts to “suppress critical voices”, while Human Rights Watch said that “instead of addressing legitimate citizen concerns, institutions expected to uphold rights appear to be under the stranglehold of rising authoritarianism.”

The Indian mission to the UN in Geneva, however, called the global concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.

It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution.

“As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order.”

As youth leaders have pledged to continue the protest against the election commissioner, analysts say the movement is “not going to die”.

“I don’t think the Modi government realises the extent of public anger,” Jayati Ghosh, a former professor from the Jawaharlal Nehru University, told Al Jazeera.

Ghosh said that the way the government is responding to the protests is making things much worse. “And more and more people feel alienated and oppressed by the government,” she said.

“So I don’t think this is going to end quickly, unless the government changes tack and actually starts listening and behaving like a normal democratic government.”

Veteran journalist Sanjay Kapoor says the government believes that the protests are aimed at “toppling the government”.

It may or may not happen, he added. But Prime Minister Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, he says, see the protest similar to “the colour revolutions that swept parts of eastern Europe and protests in India’s neighbourhood [Nepal and Bangladesh].”

Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst, compared the current protests to the mass protests in the 1970s that led to the declaration of the state of emergency by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

“Every time there is unrest, calling elections and the change of regime has happened,” Kidwai told Al Jazeera.

“Stopping the protests and detaining people will prolong the protests. What I am foreseeing is chaos and uncertainty.”

articles.title: Tiger kills man who entered its enclosure at English wildlife park
articles.summary: LONDON — A man died Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said.
articles.body: LONDON — A man died Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said. Emergency medical personnel responded to the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster after the incident was reported at about 1:35 p.m., but the victim died at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said in a statement. The tiger was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident, the force said. The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack and officers remained at the scene Saturday night as they investigated. “We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,’’ the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website. Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its “Land of the Tigers” attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is a purpose-built 2-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-yard raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or play in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.

articles.title: Wisconsin couple rejects $131,000 offer for proposed data centre power line that threatens their trees, six buildings and puts 130-foot tower near their driveway
articles.summary: Wisconsin homeowner Jerry Zelenka has rejected a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC).
articles.body: Wisconsin homeowner Jerry Zelenka has rejected a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC). The money was offered for a proposed power line that would cross his property in Fredonia, Wisconsin, to supply electricity to a planned data centre in nearby Port Washington. Zelenka said the latest proposal calls for clearing mature trees, demolishing six buildings and placing a 130-foot transmission tower near his driveway.​The company has offered $81,000 in compensation for the property impacts, along with an additional $50,000 one-time payment if he signs an agreement now. The 75-year-old homeowner, who bought the land with his wife in 1990, said the proposed changes would leave their house standing while removing much of the property they have built and maintained over the years.Proposed power line threatens trees and buildings​Zelenka said ATC's latest proposal follows an earlier application that, according to him, the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin deemed incomplete. The company has since submitted a new application with revised plans and routes.​Under the current proposal, Zelenka said, a stretch measuring about 1,000 feet long and 75 feet wide would be cleared of trees and vegetation. The affected trees include cedar, oak, ash, elm and black walnut. He also said the project would require removing a shed, chicken coop, hog barn, antique barn, garage, and machine shed.​“The point is that everything from that fence all the way to the road is clear-cut,” Zelenka said. “And after they clear-cut it, then they want to spray herbicide and just kill everything between my house and the highway.”​The proposed tower and high-voltage lines would also change the property's surroundings, potentially affecting its value.​“My house is right there. The only thing that’s left standing is the house,” he said.​Homeowner questions $131,000 compensation offer​Zelenka said the proposed compensation wouldn't cover the cost of replacing the buildings or adequately account for the impact on the property's value. He also objected to the additional payment being conditional on signing an agreement immediately.“You know, the bribe in a sense is that if I were to sign up now, they’re offering $50,000 more,” Zelenka said.The homeowner said relocating was not a realistic option for him and his 73-year-old wife, who has advanced Parkinson’s disease. The couple built their home after buying the land in the winter of 1990, spending nine months on the house while living in a shed.​Zelenka said he would not voluntarily accept the proposal and raised concerns that ATC could use eminent domain to acquire the property if they could not reach an agreement.​“If they decide they’re going to go this way, they can file for eminent domain, they’ll condemn the property, and there’s nothing I can do about it,” Zelenka said. “Then they’ll make an offer for whatever they feel is acceptable, and my only option at that point is I can fight them in court for a higher value, but I can’t stop the land seizure.”​Dispute over data centre power line continues​Zelenka questioned whether the proposed transmission line qualifies for eminent domain, arguing it would primarily serve a private data centre rather than the general public. He said two neighbouring property owners who are attorneys are challenging the issue in federal court. The legal outcome and the project's final route remain uncertain.The homeowner also said changing proposals and compensation offers made ATC's plans hard to understand.​“The thing that’s really frustrating is trying to get the truth or accurate information,” he said. “First we get offers and then the offers are pulled and we think they’re routing another way… then, oop… now they’re sending new offers.”​Zelenka said he intends to continue opposing the proposed route rather than accept the compensation and fight it in court.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mysterious find beneath field leads man to massive treasure hidden for centuries
articles.summary: Marking the largest coin hoard from Emperor Hadrian's era ever found, a metal detector hobbyist unearthed 934 Roman silver denarii near Cologne, Germany.
articles.body: A man searching a German field with a metal detector stumbled upon a remarkable discovery. He found 934 ancient Roman silver coins — and an expert says the nearly 2,000-year-old treasure and "huge hoard" may have been someone's life savings. The coins, found near Wesseling, south of Cologne, were uncovered by Oliver Riedl, according to The Associated Press (AP). Though the hoard was discovered last year, officials only recently announced the find, calling it the largest coin hoard from the reign of Roman Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany. PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE A licensed metal detectorist, Riedl immediately alerted archaeological authorities after realizing more coins were buried beneath the surface. The hobbyist told the AP he suspected there were more coins beneath the surface after his metal detector continued picking up signals. "It was clear to me there was something bigger buried here," he said. Pictures show the ancient Roman silver denarii after they were carefully cleaned, some bearing portraits and inscriptions. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ANCIENT SITE DURING RAIL PROJECT, INCLUDING RARE ROMAN FIND The coins were likely buried intentionally between 125 and 150 A.D., according to the LVR Office for the Preservation of Archaeological Monuments in the Rhineland. The staggering hoard weighs 6.8 pounds and is currently on display at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn. The most striking aspect of the hoard was its unusual size, said Johannes Wienand, a professor of ancient history at the Technical University of Braunschweig in Germany. Wienand was not involved in the discovery or its research but told Fox News Digital the hoard is "a huge treasure." POLICE OFFICERS SPOT STRANGE OBJECTS UNDERWATER, THEN MAKE REMARKABLE ANCIENT DISCOVERY "It's certainly the largest Roman coin hoard of that sort from Hadrian's time," he said. "It's a time capsule of the money the people in that period actually used day by day." "A Roman soldier would need six, seven, eight, even more years to save this amount of money, maybe for his retirement." A Roman legionary would have earned a gross salary of around 300 denarii per year, Wienand said, meaning the hoard was roughly equivalent to three years of a soldier's gross salary. "A Roman soldier would need six, seven, eight, even more years to save this amount of money, maybe for his retirement," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The coins were discovered in a rural area near the Rhine frontier, which marked a border of the Roman Empire at the time, he noted. The Roman city of Cologne and a legionary fortress in Bonn were also nearby — raising the possibility of a military connection. While a military connection is possible, Wienand said the identity of the hoard's owner remains unknown. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It seems to have been the life savings of one person who put this treasure together and put it in a pot, buried it in the soil to save it for later," Wienand said. "And obviously the owner was never able to recover this treasure." Above all, Wienand said the discovery highlights the importance of responsible metal detecting and reporting archaeological finds. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It's actually a story of how to do things right," he said. "The metal detectorist was licensed. He had permission to look for finds like that. He immediately called the heritage officers." Wienand added, "He reported the find, and he contributed to an orderly exploration of this remarkable find." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "These coins and this hoard [are] now part of our cultural heritage. And I think that's a very good outcome of this story." The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: California city backs down on $20K daily fine threat against pastor's food pantry after outpouring of support
articles.summary: Matt Mahan says San Jose is offering relocation help to Lighthouse Food Rescue after a citation threatened daily fines of up to $20,000 a day.
articles.body: A California pastor who provides free groceries to more than 1,000 people daily was ordered in September to shut down his food pantry after the city of San Jose cited zoning violations and blocked sidewalks, threatening fines of up to $20,000, just a day before officials changed course following an outpouring of social media support. Lighthouse Food Rescue & Distribution, operated by Pastfor Ralph Olmos, received a citation requiring the nonprofit to remove its food distribution operation from the public sidewalk within 10 days and cease operations at its longtime 17th Street location within 60 days. Olmos told Fox News Digital that despite the city's subsequent offer to help with relocation costs, he sees little possibility of keeping the pantry at its current location, pointing to the city's previous recognition of his charitable work. "I can tell you that this is definitely not my first rodeo with the City," Olmos told Fox News Digital. "But from being called a Beacon of hope, to get out or we will fine you. There really doesn't seem any way that the Lighthouse stays on 17th street." CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR CANDIDATE WARNS OF 'MAGA-LIKE' STATE MOVEMENT UNLESS DEMS 'WAKE UP' Following the backlash, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan and Councilmember Anthony Tordillos, who represent the district where Lighthouse operates, told Fox News Digital that the city was working to help relocate the pantry while addressing concerns about sidewalk accessibility for neighborhood residents. "Two things can be true at once – and they are in this case. Lighthouse is doing incredible work in the community and their neighbors deserve to be able to use the sidewalk," the officials said in a joint statement. "We’ve been working with our Housing Department and Code Compliance Team to find a place where the pastor can relocate and continue serving the community while ensuring that the mobility issues in the neighborhood are addressed so that elderly and disabled residents can get where they need to go," they added. The officials also addressed the potential financial penalties outlined in the city's original enforcement notice, emphasizing that no fines had been imposed and that San Jose was instead offering financial assistance to help the nonprofit relocate. "No fines have been assessed – in fact, the City has offered to help with relocation costs because we are committed to finding a solution that is not punitive but creates a better situation for everyone involved," Mahan and Tordillos said. DEM MAYOR FED UP WITH HOMELESS CRISIS PROPOSES JAILING VAGRANTS WHO REFUSE HOUSING The response followed a report from San Jose Spotlight, detailing a Sept. 25 citation ordering Lighthouse to remove its sidewalk food distribution operation and canopies within 10 days or face potential fines of up to $20,000 daily. The citation also directed the nonprofit to cease operations at its current location within 60 days. Pastor Ralph Olmos, the nonprofit's president and CEO, previously expressed concern about abandoning the families who depend on its services. "I'm up against the wall. It's almost like (the city is) telling me to stop. But my conviction says, 'How can I leave the people?'" Olmos told San Jose Spotlight. The pantry, located near East Julian and North 17th streets, distributes groceries five days a week to families, seniors, homeless residents and people with disabilities. Its offerings include milk, meat, eggs and specialized food packages. WATCH: CALIFORNIA DEMS RALLY AROUND HEALTHCARE FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS DURING FIERY DEBATE Mahan also addressed the controversy on Instagram, saying his administration was working to ensure the organization's charitable efforts continue. "Seeing the outpouring of advocacy and support for [Light House Food Rescue] has been amazing — and I’m right there with you. Pastor Olmos has been doing incredible work in our community and we’re going to make sure that work can continue. My team, alongside our Housing Department, has been in touch with the Pastor over the past week to help them relocate to a location that works for them, the people they serve and their neighbors. The city may even be able to help them with moving costs. Stay tuned!" Mahan said. The controversy marked another dispute between the Lighthouse and the city. In 2022, the nonprofit faced a special use permit requirement costing up to $15,500. Following community opposition, then-Mayor Sam Liccardo and Councilmember Raul Peralez proposed waiving or funding the fees. The City Council later voted unanimously to support relief for food pantries, according to the San Jose Spotlight. That same year, San Jose officially recognized Lighthouse through its Silicon Valley Strong Heroes initiative, praising Olmos and volunteers for feeding vulnerable residents during the pandemic. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP City Planning, Building and Code Enforcement spokesperson Marika Krause told San José Spotlight that zoning rules have since changed and a special use permit is no longer available for the pantry's current operations. The city has not publicly confirmed a finalized relocation site or whether the original 60-day shutdown order has been rescinded.

articles.title: Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
articles.summary: IRGC warns against ignoring waterway’s ‘security and rules’ as CENTCOM says US disabled vessel trying to run blockade.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Strikes around the strategic Strait of Hormuz have picked up again as mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Saturday night that an unnamed crude oil supertanker hit a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route in the waterway with navigation systems turned off. In a statement, it warned of a similar fate for any oil tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.

On Sunday, a senior Iranian army official told state television that the country’s forces remain prepared for both defensive and offensive operations, more than seven months since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran on February 28.

“We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” said Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint coordinator of the army.

His comments came after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several incidents of military action or warnings against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman over the past day. It said ship masters in the vicinity of Ras al-Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), had been directed via radio broadcast overnight to move from their anchorages. And on Sunday afternoon, UKMTO reported ⁠an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker ⁠heading outbound through the Strait of ⁠Hormuz.

Separately, the UAE said its coastguard had rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out at an unnamed tanker close to its shores, although it did not identify the cause of the blaze.

Early on Sunday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) released footage of a fighter jet bombing the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and disabling its propulsion to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports .

Since the US reimposed the blockade in mid-July, CENTCOM says its forces have disabled four commercial vessels, turned around 135 ships and destroyed 10 tankers linked with Iran. Washington says Tehran has exported no oil through the blockade line.

This comes as at least a dozen ships were attacked over the week ending on October 5, the highest number since the war began. At least one was hit off the north coast of Qatar , signalling that the danger extends beyond the immediate Hormuz passage as Iran and the US vie for control.

The ship attacks appear to have decreased energy flows that had surpassed pre-war levels at the start of the month. Kpler data cited by CNBC on Friday showed that average crude passing through the strait for the week ended October 7 was 8.5 million barrels per day, roughly 40 percent below the normal level.

To reopen the strait and reach a resolution to the war, Iran has demanded a return to a now-collapsed memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June, as well as Washington’s backing of an already finalised Iran-Oman deal that designates temporary coordinated entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the strait.

Messages continue to be exchanged between the two sides through mediators, although no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks leading to the US midterm vote, set to take place on November 3, and Israel’s election, due on October 27.

US Vice President JD Vance said last week that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the war, signalling a potential easing of the oft-repeated US demand that zero enrichment must take place on Iranian soil.

Tehran has said a nuclear agreement potentially involving diluting its high-enriched uranium can be part of the later stages of talks, but has emphasised it will not abandon enrichment altogether.

“The achievements of our indigenous nuclear industry cannot be stopped,” Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said during a speech on Sunday, pointing to electricity generation as a main use case.

He also renewed criticism against the International Atomic Energy Agency for not condemning repeated US threats to again bomb Iran’s nuclear facilities .

Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, told reporters on Sunday that authorities plan on using military and diplomatic avenues to get what they want.

“The Islamic Republic will decisively pursue the country’s interests,” he said. “If those interests can be secured through diplomacy, that is much better, but if not, we will secure them in the field of battle”.

articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
articles.summary: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, threatening fragile peace in the region.
articles.body:
Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.

The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.

The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.

However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.

So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?

What did Eritrea and Ethiopia say at the UN?

Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.

In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.

He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.

Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.

Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.

He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.

The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.

Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.

Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.

“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.

Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.

Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts.

“Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera.

He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said.

“The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.”

What is the latest fighting about, and how is Eritrea allegedly involved?

Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.

The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city.

In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.

Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.

It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.

Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims.

The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development.

Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified.

The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.

That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018.

Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.

The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated.

Has Ethiopia sent troops north towards Eritrea?

Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday.

Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city.

Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops.

Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat.

Are Ethiopia and Eritrea inching towards war?

Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation.

BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.”

He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”.

Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours.

Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera.

“The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted.

“It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.”

Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.

“The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control.

“A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.

articles.title: At least 139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti
articles.summary: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
articles.body: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations. The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said. Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el Mandeb strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement. That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait. “This is a devastating loss of life,” said Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.” “No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” IOM Director General Amy Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.” Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project.

articles.title: ‘People want change’: Sachin Pilot says Congress will return to power in Punjab with absolute majority
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary in-charge of Punjab Sachin Pilot on Sunday expressed confidence that his party would return to power in the state
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary in-charge of Punjab Sachin Pilot on Sunday expressed confidence that his party would return to power in the state with an absolute majority, claiming that people had lost faith in the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government and wanted a change.Speaking to reporters at the Punjab Congress headquarters in Chandigarh, Pilot said voters wanted to bring the Congress back to power in the Assembly elections scheduled for early next year.“The Congress will form its government with absolute majority in Punjab,” Pilot said, alongside newly appointed Punjab Congress president Pargat Singh, according to news agency PTI.Singh, a three-time MLA from Jalandhar Cantt and former captain of the Indian hockey team, formally took charge as the Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) president at a ceremony at Punjab Congress Bhawan on Sunday.He replaced Ludhiana MP Amrinder Singh Raja Warring, who stepped down from the post earlier this month.Pilot acknowledged Warring's work during his four-and-a-half-year tenure as state Congress president and said Singh had now been entrusted with the responsibility of leading the party's state unit.“Pargat Singh has assumed his charge. Former Punjab Congress president Amrinder Singh Raja Warring worked very hard for four-and-a-half years. Now, Pargat Singh has been entrusted with the responsibility,” Pilot said.Pilot says Punjab voters want ‘badlav’Pilot said Congress leaders were working together ahead of the Assembly elections, adding that four months remained for the polls.“People of Punjab have lost faith in AAP government and want 'badlav'. They want to get rid of this government,” he said, expressing confidence that voters would bring the Congress back to power.Singh, meanwhile, called for collective efforts to address the state's challenges.“We all will have to work hard together. The Punjab brand needs to be fixed...,” he said.Former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi, who attended the event, said he would highlight issues concerning Punjab under the AAP government. He accused the state government of allowing drugs and gangsterism to flourish and alleged that it had damaged the state's economy. Channi also claimed that corruption and mafia activity were prevalent in the state.Congress MP Manish Tewari called for unity within the party, saying its leaders would work together to address Punjab's concerns, news agency ANI reported.Pilot raises ‘vote chori’ allegationsPilot also criticised the BJP over the opposition's demand for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls.“I am surprised that we are seeking resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar. If we ask questions from the CEC, why are BJP spokespersons giving a reply... Why are BJP spokespersons defending him? It has been proved beyond doubt that there has been 'vote chori' in the country, responsibility of murdering democracy lies on them and the government has aided them,” he said.Pilot claimed that the names of 13 crore voters had been deleted and said irregularities in elections would prompt a public response.“Today, public is on roads and there is anger among the youth. Names of 13 crore voters have been cut. When irregularities will be committed in polls, so there will be reaction from public,” he said.He added that Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge stood with the people and democracy.Warring pledges support to new state chiefWarring, who resigned as Punjab Congress president on October 1, said he would support Singh and continue working for the party, PTI reported.“There is no other objective. Raja Warring may have lost and fallen, but my job is to keep holding the party flag high,” he said.Warring also acknowledged that some party leaders had opposed him during his tenure and might continue to do so, but insisted that he would not oppose the new leadership.“I only consider Rahul Gandhi as my leader,” he said, adding that he would remain a Congress worker regardless of whether he received a ticket for the next Assembly elections.The Congress leadership changed the state unit's leadership ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections amid internal disagreements over the organisation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
