articles.title: Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
articles.summary: Repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Airport reveal the limitations of even high-tech air defences.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), are hitting deep inside Saudi Arabia with waves of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.

Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times by the Houthis since their new military campaign against the kingdom began in September.

An attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded 309, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority was forced to suspend operations and diverted all flights, while the United States and United Kingdom issued new travel warnings for citizens.

The Houthis claimed two other attacks on the air hub earlier this week and on Sunday warned people to avoid Saudi airports.

Saudi Arabia possesses one of the best-equipped militaries in the world, boasting advanced, multilayered air defence systems.

Saudi warplanes have pummelled Houthi positions across Yemen in the past week, seeking to roll back the Iran-backed group’s recent advances against the Yemeni government army, which Riyadh supports.

The Houthis’ own arsenal has come a long way since the group seized control of Sanaa from the government in September 2014.

Their drones and missiles have reached as far as Israel and, as their accuracy has shown, can hit particular targets such as Saudi airports and oil facilities.

Here’s what we know about the Houthis’ weaponry, how their tactics have changed and why Saudi air defences are struggling to keep pace.

The exact type of weapon used to attack Riyadh airport is unknown, but the Houthis have fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the 2015 intervention. The Iran-backed group has also targeted Israel and allegedly Israeli-linked vessels since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.

The group has used its weapons in concert, mixing drones and missiles of varying speeds to confound air defences. The same mix has shaped Yemen’s ground war, with the Houthis pounding government positions for weeks before seizing the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month.

Among the group’s most advanced options are medium-range ballistic missiles such as the Palestine-2, a two-stage solid fuel missile believed to have a range of 2,000km with hypersonic capabilities. Another is the Toufan, which appears to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr missile , thought to have a range of between 1,350km and 1,950km.

The reach of those missiles – some carrying cluster warheads – has allowed the Houthis to breach Israel’s air defence network, some 2,000 km from Yemen.

The Houthis also maintain a number of short-range missiles, such as their Burkan and Badr series. They are also believed to be of Iranian origin and have been used in cross-border strikes into Saudi Arabia.

According to Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at Kings College War Studies Department, the Houthis’ missile arsenal is essentially derived from Iranian weaponry, with some Chinese technological influences.

“The Houthis have demonstrated little evidence of significant indigenous technological innovation,” he said. “Their domestic capabilities are largely confined to producing certain lower-end missiles and drones.”

Last month, Yemen’s government forces alleged that the Houthis have been receiving help from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to develop a new capability – loitering cruise missiles.

Why are Saudi defences struggling to keep up?

Saudi authorities say their forces shot down a number of projectiles over the past week, including a pair of ballistic missiles aimed at the capital on Thursday. But they failed to intercept the projectile that hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.

Nawaf Obaid told Al Jazeera that occasional penetration of Saudi air defences is to be expected, given the size of the kingdom and its border with Yemen.

“As much as you can have a multi-layered air defence system, one will always come through,” he said, pointing out that dozens of Houthi attempts are thwarted for each successful attack.

Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the main focus of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defence system was countering threats from Iran.

However, as the attacks from the Houthis increase, he views it as likely that the Saudis are re-orienting some of these defences towards Yemen.

There is also the issue of interceptor stocks. Saudi Arabia – along with many of the United States’ regional and global allies – has struggled with limited stockpiles of Patriot and THAAD munitions. These were rapidly expended by the US and its allies during the early months of the war with Iran.

Last month, Riyadh had reportedly reached out to a number of friendly countries to deploy air defence or other support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis.

However, the Houthis are also fighting under serious constraints. The group is under a UN-mandated arms embargo, a years-long Saudi blockade, as well as fighting on several fronts across Yemen.

“Militarily, the Saudi-led coalition has the upper hand, but the Houthis can still dominate the headlines with occasional strikes against Saudi Arabia,” Obaid said.

“As the world’s largest crude oil exporter and a G20 economy, Saudi Arabia carries global responsibilities that make such attacks disproportionately visible.”

The exact size of the Houthis’ missile arsenal is unknown, calling into question the group’s ability to sustain attacks on Saudi Arabia, while simultaneously fighting a fierce ground war where missiles and drones have been used by the Iran-backed group.

Obaid said that Saudi Arabia’s air campaign in Yemen has focused heavily on targeting the group’s missile depots, underground installations and drone production facilities. The group is “inflicting enormous damage” on the Houthis’ military capabilities, he added.

Pusztai told Al Jazeera that the Houthis likely have just a limited number of short-range ballistic missiles left.

This would mean they would be incapable of launching saturation attacks, where multiple missiles and drones are fired at targets, such as in Saudi Arabia.

Instead, they could focus on aiming single missiles at less-defended civilian targets “to maximise the strategic impact of these attacks, in this case to disrupt civilian air traffic”.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'
articles.summary: Zelensky says Kyiv would support such a truce. Moscow has yet to comment.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in their war, with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but no comment from Moscow.

The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially told a US media outlet that it was "news" to him, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He has also accused Russia of striking Ukraine's energy facilities after Trump posted his announcement.

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.

Zelensky expressed surprise about the announcement to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".

"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.

The BBC has asked the White House for further details.

French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have both expressed their support for an energy truce.

After speaking to von der Leyen, Zelensky said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power outages, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kahrkiv region.

"All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.

An earlier strike in Kharkiv killed three people in a grocery store, regional officials said.

For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.

Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".

The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.

The deal announced with Russia earlier this week, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

The US-Israeli war with Iran has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's oil products usually flow - and pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.

That conflict has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.

The deal was condemned by European allies of both the US and Ukraine.

Zelensky warned the deal would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his country, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump, in turn, accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries, while urging Ukraine to hold elections for a new leader.

Zelensky responded by pledging to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.

The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.

Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia will have to respond to Houthi airport attack - but the choices are stark
articles.summary: As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi group continues to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
articles.body: As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom. The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground. Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 12 people. Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost. The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington. After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz. “This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.” So far, Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question. Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub. Better missile capability Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv. “They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.” Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons. The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport. The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence. AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels. Seeking international support Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help. Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war. Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command. Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month, urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene. “Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.” Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis. Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war. “The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.” Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

articles.title: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.summary: Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
articles.body: PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. Simon’s eye was moving northward just off the coast, and forecasters at the U.S. National Hurricane Center said it’s not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 150 mph (240 kph). That’s not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for U.S. tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm. At daybreak, Simon was centered about 110 miles (175 kilometers) south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow 6 mph (9 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall. “Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning,” Papin told The Associated Press on Sunday. “We’re expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect,” Papin said. “They’re also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that’s likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells.” As for predicting whether Simon will make landfall, “it’s a little tricky right now” to forecast, since the eye “is basically moving very close or parallel to the coast currently,” Papin said. But he predicted that Cabo Corrientes is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system on Sunday. Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 centimeters) of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters). “This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the center warned. Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers as well as visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones. On Saturday, just ahead of the worst weather, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows. The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge. Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans. “Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully,” he said of what the couple would do. “I just don’t know what to expect.”

articles.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire, but Zelenskyy says this is ‘news for me’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict.
articles.body: President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict. There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly said this “was news for me.” Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to continue their aerial attacks on each other’s energy facilities. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” He did not elaborate further on what the ceasefire might include. Zelenskyy told Axios that he knew nothing about a ceasefire deal. “But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree,” Zelenskyy said, according to Axios. “If President Trump negotiated it with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it.” NBC News has reached out to Zelenskyy’s office for further comment. It follows a dramatic few days in which Trump agreed to a diesel deal with the Kremlin, demanded Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. The shift left Kyiv and its European allies reeling. The U.S. agreed Friday to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal that Trump said would see Russia “immediately” release 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and global marketplace,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that. After strong criticism from Zelenskyy, Trump said Saturday: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals.” Trump has sought to blame the Ukraine conflict, rather than his own assault on Iran, for a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices to record highs since the U.S. launched the Middle East war in February. Zelenskyy reiterated Sunday that he was ready to halt strikes on Russian refineries if the Kremlin halts its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. “We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy — both sides,” he said in interview on ABC News’ “This Week.” He added that if Russia wants an energy ceasefire, “we are open for this.” “Don’t attack us,” he said. “Don’t kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel.” The Ukrainian president also told ABC News he would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy said “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to ​change who is ​leading Ukraine. He ⁠said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel ​prices “when everybody in the world understands [that] ​because ⁠of the war in [the] Middle East, the prices are rising.” Zelenskyy was also asked on ABC News why Trump and Elon Musk blamed the Ukrainian president for the war’s continuation. “Because these people can’t find a key how to stop Putin, because it’s more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others, because it’s more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine,” he responded, pointing to how the war in Iran was leading to higher fuel prices.

articles.title: How the ICC can be saved
articles.summary: Hoping for ‘dialogue’ with the US over its sanctions on the ICC is meaningless. Action is needed to protect the court.
articles.body:
The sanctions the United States has imposed on the International Criminal Court threaten to degrade its capacity to function, leaving it to die a slow institutional death. Its continued operation as an international organisation, let alone a court of law, would become impossible.

The international community has responded with weak statements of condemnation. States Parties have had more than 20 months since US President Donald Trump came to power to prepare for this move. Efforts should have been made to strengthen the court’s institutional resilience.

Still, it is not too late to act. The grace period offered by the US should be used not to engage in fruitless negotiations, but to undertake immediate measures to protect the court.

The sanctions block the ICC’s assets and other property interests in the US or in the possession or control of US persons. Subject to exemptions and licences issued by the US Department of the Treasury, US individuals and companies are prohibited from doing business with the court.

US banks, insurers, IT firms, and other businesses cannot supply the ICC with goods or services or receive payments from it without risking penalties. Many non-US businesses will overcomply and withhold their services out of fear of being sanctioned themselves.

Cutting the court off from suppliers and service providers could paralyse its investigative and prosecutorial activities across all situations.

The sanctions, however, come with a “grace period” of 180 days to allow for maintaining or winding down the ICC operations. This covers States Parties’ payments to the ICC, salary payments, health insurance, and medical services for its employees or contractors, and payments for rent, utilities, and routine services. Separate licences permit the provision of certain telecommunication, cloud and software services, the processing of ICC pension payments, and services needed for the benefit of specified ICC detainees.

Washington has presented the “grace period” as an opportunity for States Parties “to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions” addressing US objections. Yet, in essence, it is an instrument of overt political coercion designed to force States Parties into compliance.

After the sanctions announcement, numerous States Parties once again reaffirmed their support for the court and criticised the US. At this point, however, the ICC cannot be defended with statements alone.

Performative support rings hollow unless accompanied by a coherent, coordinated strategy for countering US coercion and protecting the ICC’s independence. Declarations will not prevent banks from closing ICC accounts, insurers from withdrawing coverage, tech companies from discontinuing their services, or other businesses from abandoning the court out of fear of US retaliation.

The European Union has repeatedly affirmed that the ICC is a cornerstone of international justice and that its independence from external pressure must be protected. On October 10, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas reiterated this position, calling attacks or threats against the court, its officials, and those cooperating with it “not acceptable”.

Beyond these statements, however, the EU has remained passive, seemingly out of fear of further antagonising Trump and triggering US tariffs.

It is troubling that some States Parties and the EU have welcomed the humiliating “grace period” as creating “scope for dialogue” and “space for diplomacy” with Washington. What meaningful compromise is possible when the US objective, stated in unequivocal terms, is to destroy the court?

Over the past 20 months, the US has steadily escalated its war on the ICC. For States Parties and the EU to expect a different outcome now is an exercise in self-deception that betrays, in equal measure, obsequious deference to Washington and a lack of self-respect. Appeasing bullies only emboldens them.

Dialogue under such coercive conditions opens the door to pressure on the ICC to retreat from its mandate in Palestine in exchange for sanctions relief. Accepting US demands, in particular sacrificing the Palestine investigation to appease the rogue regime in Washington, would destroy the court as an independent and impartial institution.

It would reinforce the perception that international justice operates selectively, depending on the political power of those within its purview. Betraying the ICC’s mandate and victims’ pursuit of justice would mean an intolerable loss of legitimacy for the court and discredit the very idea that no one is above the law.

Meaningful action is long overdue, but it is not too late for it. States Parties must now make a principled choice and stick to it. They must defend the ICC and secure its ability to function – not pursue fruitless dialogue with a hostile non-party state, beg it for mercy, and offer concessions neither they nor the court can afford.

They must publicly commit to increasing the ICC’s budget and provide it with the resources and facilities it needs to withstand political and economic pressure. They must adopt effective legal measures, blocking legislation and safeguards against financial de-risking, to shield the court, its officials, and those cooperating with it from the extraterritorial effects of US sanctions. These protections must extend equally to Palestinian civil society organisations, targeted for supporting the court’s investigations.

The EU should immediately activate its Blocking Statute to prohibit EU operators from complying with US sanctions. Although no silver bullet, this measure would go some way towards shielding the ICC. A growing number of Member States and MEPs have called on the European Commission to extend this legislation to the anti-ICC sanctions and ensure that protections would be in place in the event of court-wide sanctions. This step can no longer be postponed.

In parallel, States Parties must urgently finalise arrangements for alternative banking, payment and digital infrastructure to ensure the court’s uninterrupted access to essential services. The measures must form a coordinated, structural response, going beyond declarations of solidarity and temporary fixes.

If the international community stands by as the US dismantles the ICC, the ability of any international court — or even any national court — to operate without fear or favour will become impossible.

The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Isaias moves north into Appalachians and mid-Atlantic; Southern California battered by Rachel
articles.summary: PENSACOLA, Fla. — As people in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up in the wake of Isaias, the storm’s remnants brought heavy rainfall and the risk of flooding across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region on Sunday.
articles.body: PENSACOLA, Fla. — As people in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up in the wake of Isaias, the storm’s remnants brought heavy rainfall and the risk of flooding across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region on Sunday. Meanwhile, rain and waves from Tropical Storm Rachel battered Southern California. In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. Tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina, and life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts. The remnants of a separate storm — Rachel — were expected to bring heavy rains and gusty winds to parts of the southwestern U.S., according to the National Hurricane Center. At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. The first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north. In Florida’s Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from 4 to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said. One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city’s fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency. Heavy rains cause problems in North Carolina In Burke County, North Carolina, officials said there were at least two water rescues. An unhoused male and female were camping when floodwaters from the Catawba River caught them off guard. They were rescued, along with their dog, according to a spokesperson for the county emergency management agency. Separately, a woman trapped inside her car in floodwaters was freed outside of Morganton. In McDowell County, North Carolina, just west of Burke County, first responders said they dealt with five landslides and voluntary evacuations overnight Saturday into Sunday as they responded to flooded roads and streams overflowing their banks. “Despite a challenging night, we are thankful to report no known injuries or loss of life. We call that a success!” the county emergency management agency posted online. Nearly a dozen local weather stations in the western North Carolina county reported torrential 24-hour rainfall totals at 9 a.m. Sunday, from about 5 inches (13 centimeters) to as much as 9.57 inches (24 centimeters) at the fire/rescue station in Enola. The National Weather Service said rainfall was diminishing in the area but that rapid river rises and flooding remained possible. Dealing with Isaias aftermath in Florida Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage.” The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach. Jennifer Lynne Williams, 56, was killed during the storm, her husband, Joey, told NBC News. He was distraught as he explained that a tree hit their Pensacola home, crushing their family room and killing his wife instantly. He described his wife as a kind soul and they rescued dogs together. It’s hard to envision the rest of his life without her, he said. “Why her?” he said. “How am I supposed to go on?” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis confirmed there were two fatalities in the state, one from a tree falling on a home and another related to running a generator inside a garage. There were no other reports of fatalities as of Sunday afternoon. There are more than 16,000 workers out in crews focusing on power restoration, he added. Roughly 356,000 customers were without power Sunday at 2 p.m. ET in southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, according to poweroutage.com. “They’re going to work into the night and have virtually everything to be restored by sometime tomorrow, as is their current schedule,” DeSantis said. There could be river flooding possible in the upcoming days, the governor warned. It was fortunate that the area did not see the level of storm surge that officials prepared for, but DeSantis noted that there was significant damage from the wind gusts. “I would just urge people to be very careful,” DeSantis said. “There’s a lot of debris out there, particularly as you get to the northern part of panhandle. A lot of trees knocked down, a lot of hazards. There may be still power lines knocked down.” At a church in Pensacola where the United Cajun Navy was distributing supplies Sunday morning, a line of hundreds of cars stretched around the block. Yvette Haro said she arrived at 5 a.m. after being turned away the previous day because supplies had run out. With a 10-year-old son and a 5-year-old daughter at home, she said it’s hard to go to stores and wait in long lines. She was looking for water, paper towels, toilet paper and cleaning supplies. “Anything that they’re willing to give us is helpful,” she said. While her home didn’t suffer any damage, the loss of electricity was making things difficult, Haro said. “The biggest thing is our food going bad. It’s really hard to keep grilling everything and then where do we store all this food?” Rachel brings wind and rain to southern California Rachel became a post-tropical cyclone overnight, bringing damaging rain and waves to southern California. Waves from the storm battered a century-old wooden boardwalk on the Long Beach peninsula and forced homeowners to evacuate over the weekend. The strip of multimillion-dollar oceanfront properties, along with much of the Southern California coastline, was already reeling from Hurricane Marie in September. Jake Gordon, a Long Beach real estate agent, said he was devastated to see the historic boardwalk in his hometown reduced to a splintered pile of wood amid ongoing erosion from storm surges. “This area is completely shattered and vulnerable,” Gordon said. “The fact that Rachel came and gave it the knockout blow — I don’t want to say it can’t get any worse for these houses, but it’s really, really sad.” Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said that the storm would affect the whole city, and urged city residents to avoid the peninsula through the weekend as crews worked to clean up the area. More than half a dozen houses along the coast were declared structurally unsafe. “It is not normal that we see this type of activity, especially for our residents in the peninsula,” Richardson said Saturday. “These kind of impacts are not normal, they are unprecedented for our community.” And in the Pacific, Hurricane Simon was a Category 4 storm as it approached Mexico’s coast Sunday. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

articles.title: In 2021, Joe Biden restored boundaries at two Utah monuments; more than 2 million acres regained federal protection
articles.summary: In a historic move, President Biden has restored the boundaries of Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears National Monuments, re-establishing protections for over 2 million acres that were previously reduced during Trump's administration. Learn about the implications of this restoration and the ongoing legal battles surrounding these landmarks.
articles.body: The Antiquities Act lets presidents protect federal lands and waters that hold objects of historic or scientific interest. The Congressional Research Service’s 2021 review, National Monuments and the Antiquities Act, documents the history of presidential monument designations under the law. It also notes that designations apply only to lands owned or controlled by the federal government and remain subject to valid existing rights. Two of the monuments in Utah have been a part of the dispute. President Bill Clinton established Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in Utah on September 18, 1996, through a presidential proclamation under the Antiquities Act. Both monuments have had their boundaries changed since then; this article explains what happened when they were restored in 2021 and what followed.Trump’s December 2017 proclamations removed 2.01 million acres from the two monumentsThe US Department of the Interior’s October 2021 press release states that President Barack Obama established Bears Ears National Monument in Utah in 2016, covering approximately 1.35 million acres. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on December 4, 2017, that cut the monument by 1.15 million acres, or nearly 85 percent. When combined, the two areas reduce to 2.01 million acres, not specified in the Department's release. Five Tribes and other stakeholders brought legal action against the reduction of Bears Ears, while paleontologists and conservation groups protested against the Grand Staircase reduction.Interior’s June 2021 report recommended restoring both monumentsThe Department’s Report on Restoring National Monuments responded to Executive Order 13990, signed on 20 January 2021. It describes tribal consultations on February 26 and March 1, 2021, and Secretary Deb Haaland’s visit to Utah from April 7 to 9, 2021. The report concluded that restoring the boundaries and conditions that existed on January 20, 2017, was appropriate. The Interior Department’s report recommended restoring Grand Staircase-Escalante to its January 2017 boundaries and Bears Ears to the lines Obama set, while keeping about 12,000 acres that Trump added. The October 2021 Bears Ears proclamation, published in the Federal Register, gives the exact figure as approximately 11,200 acres.The Department’s release dated October 7, 2021, announced proclamations for the next day. These proclamations restored the original Bears Ears boundaries, retained the around 11,200 added acres, and restored the Bears Ears Commission of Tribal representatives. The Interior Department’s October 7, 2021 release said the new proclamation restored Grand Staircase-Escalante to the boundaries in place in January 2017. All these 2021 proclamations have re-established protection of around 2.01 million acres that were revoked in 2017.Utah leaders asked for a legislative solutionThe report by the Interior also includes opposing views. As discussed in the report presented above, the governor and congressional delegation referred to “whiplash” due to frequent changes and noted that decisions belong to Congress. The opponents worried about the restrictions on roads, motorized recreation, mining, and grazing and noted that the jobs related to recreation pay less than those in mining. Utah and two of its counties sued in August 2022, as the Natural Resources Defense Council reports, in a case known asGarfield County v. Biden. The Native American Rights Fund said a second case, Dalton v. Biden, was brought by recreation users and a mining company, and that a district court dismissed both cases in August 2023. In a divided ruling on June 23, 2026, the Tenth Circuit vacated that dismissal in part and sent the cases back to the district court, as the court’s published opinion on govinfo.gov shows. The case is now titledGarfield County v. Trump.What the Land Economics study found In Neither boon nor bane: the economic effects of a landscape-scale national monument, published in 2018 in Land Economics, Paul Jakus and Sherzod Akhundjanov examined ranching, mining and tourism trends around Grand Staircase-Escalante. The study tested whether the monument shifted the local economy away from ranching and mining and toward tourism. The researchers used both difference-in-differences and synthetic control methods to compare pre and post-designation paths for per capita income, alongside trends in ranching, mining, and tourism. They conclude that Grand Staircase-Escalante’s monument designation had no effect on regional per capita income, suggesting the economic shift was not as dramatic as either side of the policy debate claimed.Paul Jakus and Sherzod Akhundjanov examined ranching, mining and tourism trends around Grand Staircase-Escalante. The authors also embed the monument within a policy choice dilemma where landscape-level designations may limit the use of land and have a tendency to direct activities to low-wage tourism at the expense of high-wage mining and extraction. With post-designation data on ranching, mining, and tourism from the Grand Staircase-Escalante area, the authors conduct their analysis using difference-in-differences as well as synthetic control approaches without finding any impact on per capita income.Trump’s July proclamations cut both monuments again and drew a federal lawsuitAs KUER reported, President Donald Trump signed proclamations on July 13, 2026, shrinking Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument by about 90 percent and Bears Ears National Monument by 91 percent. While the governor referred to these decisions as “right-sizing,” the president claimed that the previous designations were an injustice against Utah residents. Advocates for the West stated that Grand Staircase-Escalante lost about 1.69 million acres and Bears Ears lost 1.24 million acres, nearly 3 million acres total. On September 2, 2026, the Natural Resources Defense Council, Earthjustice, and the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance filed a federal lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump’s proclamations reducing protections for Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments. The lawsuit argues that the Antiquities Act does not authorize a president to dismantle national monuments established by previous presidents.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: At least five people missing as flash floods in Nepal sweep away houses
articles.summary: Authorities urge villagers to move to safer places after a river in the central part of the country bursts its banks.
articles.body:
Flash floods have hit central Nepal, sweeping away houses and leaving at least five people missing, according to officials, weeks after devastating flooding in the country that killed hundreds.

A landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100km (62 miles) west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River on Saturday, leading to downstream flooding, authorities said.

Two women and three men were unaccounted for, and there are no reports of casualties, said the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

According to the agency, at least 82 people, including nine foreigners, have been rescued from the affected areas.

The flood swept away about a dozen houses and two suspension bridges and damaged a hydroelectric project camp, carrying some of the construction equipment away, authorities said.

A muddy torrent washed away a highway bridge connecting Gorkha with the neighbouring Dhading district, said NDRRMA Chief Executive Dharam Raj Uprety.

The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.

“We have asked villagers living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate and remain safe,” said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, Gorkha district’s most senior bureaucrat.

National disaster authorities alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.

“Please help ensure that people in at-risk areas are moved to safe locations in time and assist search and rescue operations as needed,” the NDRRMA said in a social media post.

Officials said army and police rescue personnel had reached the area and were also monitoring the situation from a helicopter.

“The flood looked similar… It was very scary, and it still feels like a nightmare for us,” said local official Laxmi Gurung of Chumnubri rural municipality.

“Our house is gone, we have no electricity… but there have been no casualties.”

Heavy rainfall in late September also triggered floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the disaster agency.

articles.title: After oil increasingly left the Gulf, Iran is trying to regain its stranglehold on shipping
articles.summary: Iran is stepping up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf in an effort to restore its leverage over the critical waterway - and possibly goad the United States into retaliating.
articles.body: Iran is stepping up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf in an effort to restore its leverage over the critical waterway. There have been more than a dozen strikes on shipping since the end of September, reducing the volume of oil transiting the strait and keeping crude prices above $100 a barrel. US President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has no plans to strike Iran before the midterm elections, where rising energy costs could play a part in his Republican Party losing the House of Representatives, the Senate – or both. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump declared on Truth Social, adding that the administration is “having productive discussions” with Tehran and that his main goal is to ensure the country does not obtain a nuclear weapon. Tehran, however, is focused on Hormuz as a “strategic red line” and is broadening its range of targets in the Gulf. Leverage over Hormuz is non-negotiable for Tehran as it weathers US pressure despite a sinking economy. But Washington has said that the principle of free navigation in international waters is inviolable, a stance echoed by Gulf states that rely on the strait for much of their trade. In one of the latest incidents, the National Guard of the United Arab Emirates said Saturday it had rescued 22 people following an oil tanker fire. Those rescued were Indian citizens – India is one of the largest suppliers of seafarers. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) – which tracks shipping incidents – has reported several other attacks in recent days. It said the master of an outbound tanker reported it was struck Saturday by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire on board. UKMTO reported another attack in the same area on Sunday, resulting in damage to the vessel. All crew members were reported safe. The navy of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed on Saturday that a supertanker carrying crude oil suffered a massive explosion after striking a naval mine while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz through a route Tehran hadn’t authorized. “No extra-regional power has the right to threaten, maintain a domineering presence, or interfere in it. The Strait of Hormuz is Iran’s strategic red line,” said the head of the IRGC, Ahmed Vahidi, in a post on X. UKMTO said Sunday it had also received a report from several ships in UAE waters that they had been directed via VHF radio messages to move from their anchorages. Iran has avoided targeting the UAE recently. Shipping analysts Ambrey said the IRGC Navy had issued a warning to six vessels anchored around 16 miles (25 kilometers) from the port of Ras al Khaimah in the UAE. “The vessels were advised to heave up anchor, exit the area immediately, and transit to Dubai anchorage,” Ambrey noted. Analysts say the rise in Iranian attacks and threats is in response to higher volumes of oil and petroleum products through the strait. They averaged about 13.1 million barrels per day at the end of September, according to Kpler, a marine data tracking service. That’s just under 80% of the 17.1 million barrels that had traveled through the strait each day before the war broke out. But flows appear to have slowed this month. Just seven tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, less than half the seven-day average and the lowest number since July 23, data from Kpler showed. However, figures are at times revised higher after ships have moved through the strait, as many switch off their identification systems to try to avoid detection. The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports, as part of a strategy of maintaining economic pressure on Iran. On Saturday it had disabled a cargo vessel in the Gulf of ⁠Oman after the ship’s crew ignored warnings and ⁠attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran. “A U.S. military ‌fighter ⁠jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision ‌munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming ⁠the crew,” US Central Command posted on X. The US blockade has been highly effective, according to analysts. September was the first month that Iran loaded no crude onto tankers since maritime data tracking service Kpler began monitoring Iranian exports in 2013. Last week, Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the current economic situation as one of the most difficult periods the country has faced. Tehran has insisted that if it can’t export its oil, its neighbors won’t be able to either. It believes it holds the initiative, given US shortages of air defense interceptors, and says its military posture has moved towards the offensive. “Both the Americans and other countries should know: As we have said before, in a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will be able to sell oil either. And if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe,” Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, said late in September. It now seems intent on turning that threat into reality.

articles.title: More than 25 years have passed since Massachusetts mother Debra Melo vanished: ‘We’re not giving up.’
articles.summary: Debra Melo was last seen on June 20, 2000, in Weymouth, Massachusetts. Despite extensive search efforts, she is still missing, and her disappearance remains under investigation.
articles.body: The year was 2000. Stage lights blazed. Music pounded. A stadium full of fans, all there for one reason: Tina Turner. Somewhere in that crowd stood two sisters: Debra Melo and Patricia White. They were there to celebrate Patricia’s 29th birthday. But Debra didn’t seem to be in a celebratory mood. “She was not herself,” Patricia told “Dateline.” “I kept saying, like, ‘What’s wrong? Are you all right?’ And she’s like, ‘Yeah, I’m fine.’ But I knew something was definitely on her mind.” On June 20, 2000, less than two weeks later, 30-year-old Debra Melo disappeared. Debra and Patricia grew up in a family with five children in Taunton, Massachusetts. Only 18 months apart, the sisters were inseparable. “We were always together playing baseball and chase and all of that fun stuff,” Patricia said. “She was just very adventurous, smart.” Patricia told “Dateline” that when Debra was in middle school, she met a young man named Luis Melo. He was a couple of years older and had just moved from Portugal. As a nonnative English speaker, Luis took a lower-level English class to learn the language. It happened to be the same class Patricia was in. “He would sit next to me, and he would tell me, ‘I’m gonna marry your sister,’” Patricia recalled. “I was like, ‘Yeah, right. She is not interested in you.’” Six months later, Patricia remembers Debra bringing Luis to their house for dinner. Their relationship blossomed from there. According to Steven DeMoura, Patricia’s ex-husband and Debra’s former brother-in-law, Debra and Luis got married in 1986 after dating for about two years. Steven and Patricia were dating at the time and attended the wedding together. “She needed her mother’s permission to be married at the age of 16,” Steven said. Debra left high school before graduating and she and Luis worked together at a local Dunkin’ Donuts. “She usually ran the front of the store and all the personnel,” Steven said. “He ran the back.” The couple eventually had two children, a girl and a boy, and were living in Taunton. Even though their adult responsibilities were time-consuming, Patricia and Debra made time to hang out. “We’d go to the movies, or we’d go do something fun, and we would just laugh,” Patricia said. “She just had this contagious laugh that once she would start laughing, then you’d start going, and we’d be in hysterics together.” Patricia says something changed in the years leading up to Debra’s disappearance. “I noticed she was very quiet, appeared somewhat depressed, very private,” she said. “Took a lot for me to get things out of her.” Patricia told “Dateline” she believes Luis was possessive. “She wasn’t really able to talk on the phone because Luis would listen to our conversations,” she said. Patricia remembers Debra telling her that she wanted to leave the relationship. “We had discussions about where she could move with the kids,” she said. Patricia last spoke to her sister on the phone on June 18, 2000. “We were planning on going out to eat on my birthday,” she said. That never happened. On June 20, Debra disappeared. “Dateline” spoke with Deputy Chief Jason Mohan of the Bristol County District Attorney Office’s homicide unit to learn more about the day Debra disappeared. On June 20, Debra and Luis worked their typical shift at Dunkin’ Donuts from 5 a.m. to 1 p.m. “They then drove around for about an hour, the husband said, looking for a farmers market, essentially killing time until her doctor’s appointment at 3,” Mohan told “Dateline.” The appointment was with a dermatologist. The couple arrived at the appointment, stayed for about an hour, and bought $400 worth of skin cream. After leaving the doctor’s office, “Luis says that they get into a fight in the car on Route 18 in Weymouth,” Mohan said. “She demands to be let out of the car. He lets her out. He drives away for a few minutes, then says he comes back and doesn’t see her.” “That is solely information from the husband and cannot be independently confirmed,” Mohan noted. Patricia told “Dateline” she didn’t learn about Debra’s disappearance until the next day, June 21, when she received a concerning call from Debra’s daughter at 11 a.m. “She said, ‘Auntie, Mom didn’t come home last night,’” Patricia recalled. “And I said, ‘What?’ because that is extremely odd for her not to be home.” Patricia says she called Luis to learn more about what happened. According to Patricia, Luis had not yet filed a missing person report when she spoke with him. Patricia began calling around the family, Debra’s friends, and nearby hospitals, without success. The family then decided to go to the Weymouth Police Department to file a missing person report. Mohan said that both Luis and Debra’s family independently reported Debra missing to police on June 21. Since Debra was from Taunton but went missing about an hour away in Weymouth, Mohan told “Dateline” that both police departments were involved in the search for Debra. Search efforts for Debra started close to home. Mohan says the police searched the couple’s house and car around June 23. “The skin cream was recovered in the car,” he noted. But several of Debra’s belongings were missing: her pocketbook, gold bracelet, a cross chain, a pinky ring with a green stone, and her wedding ring. During this time, the police also administered two polygraph tests on Luis. Mohan told “Dateline” he failed both tests. The search widened from there. Mohan says police searched multiple forested areas, combed Route 18, and checked numerous other locations. They also brought in a plane for aerial views, deployed canine units, and used a metal detector. “This was a very heavily publicized incident at the time,” he said. “There were massive searches.” Debra was nowhere to be found. Debra’s disappearance was life-changing for Patricia. “It just caused a lot of anxiety, a lot of stress, and hurt,” she told “Dateline.” “It was devastating to all of us.” For Steven, even though he and Patricia eventually divorced, Debra’s case never left his mind. “No matter where I went or who I was dating or whatever, if I got a phone call and I had to go out in the middle of the night and meet somebody because supposedly they had evidence or they had a clue or something about Debra, I went,” he said. Mohan told “Dateline” that in 2017, police received a tip about an area in Taunton that might be connected to Debra’s case. Taunton Police conducted a dig at the site. “The search revealed nothing,” he said. “Upon further scrutiny of the timeline of the tip, it did not line up with this incident.” As the investigation continues, Debra’s case faces several challenges. “The lack of physical evidence is really the biggest obstacle,” Mohan said. “And now when you combine that with the passage of time, trying to find new witnesses, or develop new leads, it can be challenging.” In 2022, the Massachusetts State Police got creative. According to NBC affiliate WJAR, the agency created a deck of playing cards featuring information about unsolved homicides and missing person cases. The decks were distributed to inmates in the hope that someone would come forward with information. Debra’s case is the Queen of Diamonds. “It’s just another way to keep Debra’s story alive and out there and to let people know that we continue to investigate the incident,” Mohan explained. “We’ve been looking at areas of the investigation even as recently as a few weeks ago.” “We do suspect foul play in this case,” Mohan said. When asked about current suspects or persons of interest, he said, “At this time, we cannot eliminate Luis Melo as a suspect in this case.” According to Mohan, when police interviewed Luis, he denied having anything to do with his wife’s disappearance. “Dateline” reached out to Luis Melo for comment but has not heard back. In 2025, for the 25th anniversary of Debra’s disappearance, the family held a remembrance for her at Memorial Park in Taunton. “We had the mayor there and I wrote a poem,” Patricia said. “It was just to keep her name out there and keep everybody aware that she is still missing and that we are still looking for her, and we’re not giving up.” “The biggest thing I’m hoping to find is closure for Debra. You know, just what happened to her, where is she?” Steven DeMoura said. “And then if justice prevails after that, then so be it.” Mohan wants the public to know that police haven’t stopped looking for Debra. Investigators are trying “to find individuals who we may not have been able to identify in 2000, specifically people who worked with both Luis and Debra Melo.” “If anybody has any information that, even if it’s small, they don’t think it’s important, I’d rather have them call us and let us determine the value of any information than not call us at all,” Mohan said. Debra has blue eyes, is around 5’2” and weighed 108 lbs. when she disappeared. Her hair was brown at the time. She was reportedly last seen wearing a blue sundress with white flowers and a white shirt underneath. Anyone with information about the disappearance of Debra Melo is asked to contact the Bristol County District Attorney’s Office at 774-627-1600. If you have a story to share with “Dateline,” please submit it here.

articles.title: He shares a name with a Cornell rape suspect. Strangers started hunting him down.
articles.summary: The messages told him he should “rot in hell” and be thrown in jail. His friends and family received a barrage of menacing threats. Subscribe to The Post Mos...
articles.body:
The messages told him he should "rot in hell" and be thrown in jail.

His friends and family received a barrage of menacing threats.

Strangers found his cellphone number and peppered his phone with abusive texts. His face was plastered across angry videos online. Even TMZ called him.

The messengers had wrongly concluded that the man was one of the seven Chi Phi fraternity members accused of participating in a 2024 gang rape at Cornell University, a case that has commanded public attention since the accuser, known as "Jane Doe," filed a civil lawsuit last month.

But the man, a graduate student in engineering at the University of Pennsylvania, never attended Cornell - he merely shares a first and last name with one of the accused men. To make matters clear, he recently changed his LinkedIn bio to read, "I do NOT go to Cornell."

As the Cornell case has fueled public debate, it has inspired a frenzy of online sleuths, who are racing to identify and expose personal information about Jane Doe and the men she has accused, a phenomenon called "doxing."

Since Jane Doe filed the lawsuit, she has faced death threats and been confronted at her home by armed police after someone made a false report, an action called swatting, according to Thomas Giuffra, her attorney.

In their rush, the digital vigilantes have made errors - falsely identifying a slew of people who are not connected to the case.

At least three other women have been misidentified as Jane Doe on social media, Giuffra said, prompting a wave of videos in which women declare, "I am Jane Doe," to show solidarity with the accuser and attempt to obscure her identity.

After the home address of a Marine Corps sergeant who shares a name with one of the accused was mistakenly added to court documents, his family received threats, said John Manly, an attorney representing his family.

The error led the New York Supreme Court judge handling the case to seal several court documents Friday and to condemn the harassment as "brash, reckless, and ultimately dangerous internet vigilantism."

The Penn grad student said he has been worried that online vigilantes might find his home address, adding that "overall, the past few weeks have taken a toll on my mental health."

The men accused in the Cornell case have not been charged, and The Washington Post is not naming them.

One man who shares a name with one of the accused, and who graduated from Cornell four years before the incident, posted a video showing messages he had received.

"You can't hide. Your future is over. You'll get exactly what you deserve, which is prison," one said. In another video, he read a message from a woman claiming to be a witch who said she placed a hex on him: "Your soul will not find peace for the rest of your life," she had told him.

The Marine sergeant's mother said she and her family have been "absolutely terrorized with threats." She said her son has received a torrent of hateful messages through social media, while she and her daughter have received phone calls and text messages, including in the middle of the night.

One person said, "I will find you." Another said, "Rope is cheap and gravity is free."

The mother said that they've tried to tell people they had the wrong person, but that people just called them liars.

People have also thrown garbage and unidentified substances in their yard, she said, including what looked like dog poop. She said it has been hard for the family to sleep.

"We really - I can't stress this enough - we really want to be left alone."

For years, online sleuths have misidentified the subjects of high-profile news events, according to University of Michigan professor Sarita Schoenebeck, who studies online harassment. A Brown University student who had been missing when pressure-cooker bombs detonated near the Boston Marathon finish line in 2013 was falsely named as the bomber by online sleuths. He had died by suicide a month before the bombing, but he was elevated as a possible suspect in the fallout.

Schoenebeck said the damage to people named by mistake can persist long after people point out the errors. "Once misinformation spreads, corrections rarely reach as many people as the original claims," she said.

There are few reliable statistics on the frequency of doxing, but Schoenebeck said people turn to such methods when "they believe the justice system has failed. However, doxing itself lacks the fact-finding, safeguards and accountability that an effective justice system requires."

There is no comprehensive national law that prohibits posting someone's personal information. Some states bar people from publishing addresses or other information with the intent to harass or harm someone. A federal law also makes it a crime to share sensitive information about certain federal officials, jurors and others to threaten, intimidate or incite violence.

Some bystanders have targeted people more distantly connected to the Cornell case. While at least two websites feature the names and photos of the accused, a longer list of fraternity members has also appeared online.

"It wasn't just seven. 50 other individuals knew what was happening and did NOTHING," one post on Facebook reads. It includes pictures of Chi Phi fraternity members.

Some of the online posts have included former members who graduated before the incident and were not part of a group chat involving the accused, and who are now facing harassment, their attorney, Adam Ford, wrote to Cornell's general counsel in a letter reviewed by The Post.

Ford said his clients have received death threats and hate mail, with some facing adverse consequences from their universities and employers, such as being put on leave.

These alumni "had nothing to do with the events surrounding Jane Doe," Ford wrote in the letter. "Nevertheless, they are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement." The letter was first reported by CBS News.

In his letter, Ford asked Cornell to provide letters to the alumni verifying that they were not part of the incident and to call on the public to stop harassing current and former members of the fraternity.

Cornell declined to comment on the letter to The Post, citing pending litigation.

The Penn student said he understands the human impulse to seek justice. "I salute those who are willing and strong enough to take matters into their own hands, especially when large organizations and institutions take too long to address an issue," he told The Post.

However, he said that his case demonstrates that it's more important than ever to fact-check sources and verify information.

"Mob mentality is real, and it can spread just as easily on social media," he said. "People just need to be mindful of the impact our words and actions can have."

CORRECTION: A man who shares a name with one of the accused posted a video saying he graduated from Cornell four years before the incident. An earlier version of this article mistakenly said it was two years prior.

articles.summary: An Iranian anti-regime protester was hanged just hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancee over a prison phone line, in a heartbreaking ceremony
articles.body: An Iranian anti-regime protester was hanged just hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancee over a prison phone line, in a heartbreaking ceremony arranged as the couple feared they might never get another chance to be together, according to a report by the New York Post.Alireza Sepahi, 25, and Mahshad Keshani, 22, were arrested during anti-government protests earlier this year. Sepahi was sentenced to death, while Keshani is serving a five-year prison term, The Times reported.With fears growing that Sepahi's execution was imminent, Keshani pushed for an informal wedding before it was too late. The couple exchanged vows over the phone on Sunday, with their fathers joining the ceremony from inside Isfahan prison.Human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi helped conduct the ceremony, reading the vows for the couple's fathers to bless. Keshani's family could offer only a copy of the Quran, a saffron rock candy and a single red rose as a traditional dowry."It was Mahshad's idea," Davoudi told The Times. "Even now, I wonder how one young woman can possess such courage."Davoudi said he had warned Keshani that the decision could not be undone, but she remained determined."She said, 'Mr Davoudi, I love Alireza,'" he recalled.When Davoudi conveyed the proposal to Sepahi, the young man broke down in tears. The moment also moved prison officers, Davoudi said."Alireza was crying, and something deeply painful and beautiful happened. Even the prison officers began to cry," he told The Times.The wedding, however, could not save Sepahi from execution.He was hanged on Monday morning, just hours after the ceremony, alongside fellow defendant Alireza Raisi, according to reports.Sepahi had narrowly escaped execution in July after suffering a heart attack on his way to the gallows. He fell into a coma but later regained consciousness, after which authorities rescheduled his execution.A final family visit on Sunday reportedly signalled that his execution was approaching, prompting Keshani to arrange the wedding.Sepahi was among 12 men accused of involvement in the deaths of four security personnel during protests at Isfahan's Alikhani Square on January 8. Human rights groups have alleged that defendants in the case were forced to make confessions under torture.The square has also been the site of public executions of protesters, drawing condemnation from rights advocates.Following Sepahi's hanging, his family was reportedly prevented from burying him in his hometown.Davoudi condemned the authorities' actions, saying the executions were an act of revenge against young people following the regime's international humiliation."I do not know how to come to terms with this," he told The Times.You use AI every day. articles.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
articles.summary: The French firm is reinventing the classic model as carmakers come under pressure from Chinese rivals.
articles.body:
French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market.

The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs.

As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028.

As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors.

Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow".

The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around.

The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs.

Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair.

The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists.

Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000.

The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor.

The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses".

By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road.

VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success.

BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades.

But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers.

Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well.

VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta.

Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense.

"It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect."

Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands.

"Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data.

In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis.

"In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says.

"The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there."

But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller.

"A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says.

"But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal."

articles.title: CJI Surya Kant rejects INDIA bloc leaders’ request for meeting over ‘vote chori’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant has rejected the INDIA bloc leaders’ request for a meeting to submit a representation on alleged “vote
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant has rejected the INDIA bloc leaders’ request for a meeting to submit a representation on alleged “vote chori”, ANI reported on Sunday. In an email response to the opposition leaders, the CJI explained the reasons for declining their request.In response to the request the CJI said that the apex court cannot interfere with the executive’s functioning on the administrative side, sources told news agency PTI. He asked the Congress leader to file a petition on the judicial side, which could be taken up on Tuesday. The CJI also said the Supreme Court was open 24x7 to citizens whose fundamental rights were violated, PTI reported.Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Rajya Sabha LoP Mallikarjun Kharge had sought an appointment with the CJI between 4pm and 5pm on Monday to submit a memorandum demanding action over alleged electoral irregularities.Rahul had announced that opposition parties, civil society groups and young people would march to the Supreme Court, seeking Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, a halt to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and a return to paper ballots.The move to approach the CJI followed a meeting between INDIA bloc leaders and President Droupadi Murmu on Friday, during which the opposition submitted a memorandum outlining four demands. These included the CEC’s resignation, scrapping assembly elections held over the past two years, suspension of the SIR exercise and restoration of paper ballots. The memorandum also sought the restoration of 13.30 crore voters allegedly deleted from electoral rolls.After the meeting, the Lok Sabha LoP said he was surprised that Murmu had not denied the opposition’s allegations of “vote chori” and had instead asked them to provide evidence. “I was shocked that the President did not deny Vote Chori. Instead, she asked us to bring her proof. We will bring her a mountain of it,” he wrote on X.The BJP subsequently attacked Gandhi over his remarks, accusing him of misrepresenting the interaction and dragging the President into a political confrontation. BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra called the Congress leader a “nalayak neta” and argued that accepting a memorandum did not amount to endorsing its contents.“The anarchist Rahul Gandhi tried to pull the President of India into the anarchism which he's trying his best to conduct on the streets of India,” Patra said.BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad also criticised the Opposition’s protests, saying the country would be governed by Parliament, not the streets. “We are not opposed to protests, but you have weaponised street protests because of your electoral defeats,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
